title: To See a Forest
text:
01 / 06, A shared map
          KAMPARPENINSULA
          What lives here? Every dot is something a person saw in the Kampar Peninsula and shared on iNaturalist.
          Scroll to see what 10,461 sightings can show us together.
        

        
          
            First, sort what people found
            Together, the sightings reveal many kinds of life.
            The sightings gather into plants, birds, insects, mammals, fungi and reptiles. One person’s photo becomes part of a much bigger picture.
          
          
            What did everyone find?
            People recorded thousands of different living things.
            The sightings now gather by taxon: the name used to identify a living thing. Together, people recorded 3,120 taxon IDs.
          
          
            The record grows
            More sightings joined the record each year.
            The first sighting here is from 2002. More people added records over time. Each new dot is another moment someone chose to share.
          
          
            Who made this record?
            Many people helped us see Kampar.
            Ninety-two people contributed to this project. Each noticed different things, visited different places and added a piece no one else could.
          
          
            Put every piece together
            Together, their sightings make one shared map.
            The dots return to the map. No one person saw all of this. The picture exists because many people contributed.
          
        
      

      
        where people shared sightings10,461 sightings
        
        
      
    
  

  
    
      What did everyone find?
      The Canopy of Life
      Each block is one taxon ID. Large blocks were recorded often. Small blocks may come from a single sighting. Together, they show the range of life people noticed.
    
    
      
      
      
      Block size shows the number of sightings, not how common something is in the forest. The available taxonomy is simplified into a broad group, a genus level name and then a taxon name.
    
  

  
    
      
        How often was each taxon seen?
        Most were seen only once or twice.
        A few taxa appear again and again. Many appear in just one or two records.
        A taxon seen once may not be rare. It may simply be hard to find, or someone may have looked only once.
        Here, “taxon” means one distinct taxon ID in the export. It does not always mean a species.
      
      
        how many times each taxon was seen
        
        few sightingsmany sightings
      
    
  

  
    
      Who added the sightings?
      Every person adds a different piece of Kampar.
      Some people shared thousands of sightings, while others shared only one or two. Each contribution helps us see a little more.
    
    
      observers with the most sightings
      
      This is not a ranking of skill or importance. It only shows how many records each person added to this project.
    
  

  
    
      
        Each person saw something different
        Who found what?
        Each line connects a person to a taxon they recorded. Together, the lines show how many different trips and interests can build one shared picture.
        The record grows because each person notices something a little different.
        These lines connect people to their records. They do not show relationships between organisms.
      
      
        active observers and often seen taxashared sightings
        
      Only the most active observers and taxa seen most often are named here, so the lines remain readable. The opening transformation still includes every sighting.
      
    
  

  
    
      Where did people go?
      Bright places are places people visited.
      Switch between taxa, sightings, people and visit days. Some places are bright because people returned many times. A dark place may simply have had fewer visits.
    
    
      
        taxa seen
        sightings
        people
        days visited
      
      
      Taxa recorded in each 5 km cell.
      Each hexagon covers a 5 km cell. This map shows where records were made; it does not show how many organisms truly live there.
    
  

  
    
      What happens when people keep looking?
      The shared record keeps growing.
      Every visit can add a new sighting. Sometimes it adds a taxon that had never appeared in this project before.
    
    
      10,461 sightings3,120 taxon IDs92 people
      
       sightings so far  taxa found so far
      A taxon is “new” here only when it first appears in this project. It may have lived in Kampar long before someone recorded it.
    
  

  
    
      
        What citizen science can do
        One sighting can becomeshared knowledge.
      
      
        This project brings together 10,461 sightings, 3,120 taxon IDs and 92 people. Each record began with a simple act: someone noticed a living thing and chose to share it.
        
          life is therethen
          a person reaches the placethen
          they notice itthen
          they record itthen
          they share it on iNaturalist
        
        The narrowing bars show the steps every record must pass through. Their widths are illustrative, not measured percentages.
        Citizen science cannot show everything. It shows what people were able to notice, record and share.
      
    
  

  
    
      Behind every dot
      Every dot began when someone met a living thing.
      A sighting may look like one small mark on a screen. It began with a real encounter: a person stopped, looked, took a photo and shared what they found.
      
      These photographs come from iNaturalist records that allow reuse. Credits and licenses are shown with each image.
    
  

  
    
      What lives in Kampar?
      We do not knoweverything.
      But together, we can see much more than any one person could.
      One more sighting joins the shared record.
